children.text: An uninhabited sandbar about 700 m long, floating off Mambajao on Camiguin's north coast. Stand on treeless white sand facing Hibok-Hibok Volcano and Mt. Vulcan — a half-day trip just 10 minutes by bangka from the Yumbing boat terminal.
Off the north coast of Camiguin, about
1.4 km

from the Yumbing shore of the provincial capital Mambajao, a single white sandbar floats in the sea. This is White Island, an uninhabited sandbar that locals also call Medan Island. There are no trees and no buildings, just white sand running about
, and its curve — like a horseshoe or a boomerang — shifts a little with every rise and fall of the tide. That is why people say the sandbar never looks quite the same twice.
What makes it special is the scenery behind the sand. Looking south, the active volcano Hibok-Hibok rises to
on the left, with the lower Mt. Vulcan on the right. Mt. Vulcan is a parasitic cone born in
when the flank of Hibok-Hibok split open, while Hibok-Hibok itself erupted repeatedly from
to
, causing heavy loss of life in
. The area around both peaks is protected as the Timpoong and Hibok-Hibok Natural Monument and was declared an ASEAN Heritage Park in
. Few places in the Philippines fit white sand in mid-ocean and deep green volcanoes into a single frame.
Getting there is simple. At the White Island boat terminal in Yumbing you pay the entrance fee and boat fare, then cross in about
10 minutes
. Boats generally run from
to
, so many travelers catch the first boat to arrive at sunrise. With no shade, drinking water or toilets on the sandbar, most visitors stay
1–2 hours
, and mornings or late afternoons are far more comfortable than midday.

It suits photographers, anyone who wants to watch the sunrise and slip into calm water, and families looking for shallow water to play in with children. Island-wide sights such as hot springs, waterfalls and Mantigue Island are covered in the
Camiguin
entry, and the cross at sea off the west coast in the
Camiguin Sunken Cemetery
entry; this guide focuses in depth on the sandbar alone.

blocks.title: Photos with two volcanoes behind you

children.text: From the sandbar, looking south, Hibok-Hibok and Mt. Vulcan stand side by side. Frame the curving waterline in the foreground and you get white sand, jade water and green volcanoes in one shot. In the morning, low-angled light falls across the volcano slopes and sharpens their outlines.
Depending on the season, the sun rises roughly between
. On the first boat you can watch the sky color over an almost empty sandbar, and the sand is still cool enough to walk barefoot.

blocks.title: Walk the sandbar end to end

children.text: About
long, the sandbar grows and shrinks with the tide. Walking to the far end takes only
10–15 minutes
, and on some days a second, smaller sandbar appears across a shallow channel. Go around low tide to see the most sand.

blocks.title: Swim in the shallow inner side

children.text: Inside the curve of the sandbar, the water is calm and shallow, good for playing with children. The outer side tends to have bigger waves, so it is safer to swim on the inner side. The water is clear enough to see the ripples in the sand at your feet.

blocks.title: Snorkel the coral along the edges

children.text: Coral and small tropical fish gather along the edges of the sandbar. At the terminal you can rent a snorkel set for about
a day and a life jacket for about
. The deeper outer side has currents, so do not swim far out.
There is not a single tree on the sandbar, so a rented umbrella is the only shade. Each costs about
, and sharing one with your group keeps the cost down. Sitting under the umbrella gazing at the volcanoes and sea is the real pleasure of this place.
The last return boat leaves around
, so it is hard to stay on the sandbar until sunset. Instead, head back to the Yumbing or Agoho shore and watch the sun set over the sea for a neat end to the day.

items.title: Half-day course (sunrise and morning)
items.subtitle: The first boat to a quiet sandbar

children.text: Leave your beach lodging in Agoho or Yumbing. The terminal is
5–10 minutes
away on foot or by tricycle; from Mambajao town, allow
15–20 minutes
Pay the entrance fee and boat fare at the ticket office and board the first boat. Agree on a return time with the boatman and remember the boat's name.
Step onto the sandbar and watch the sunrise. As the sun climbs, Hibok-Hibok and Mt. Vulcan light up one after the other.
Before the crowds arrive, take photos with the volcanoes behind you and walk to the end of the sandbar.
Swim in the shallow inner water or snorkel along the edges.
Take the boat back to the terminal before the sun gets harsh.
Freshen up at your lodging and have breakfast. Adding Ardent Hot Spring or Katibawasan Falls in the afternoon makes for a full day.
From
December to January
, when the sun rises late, sunrise comes around
, so you can set out a little later. In
May–June
, on the other hand, the sun rises around
, so missing the first boat can easily mean missing the sunrise.

items.title: Half-day course (afternoon and dusk)
items.subtitle: Timed for low tide and sunset

children.text: Check the afternoon low-tide time in a tide table and head to the terminal. The closer to low tide, the more of the sandbar is exposed.
Cross by bangka, rent an umbrella and settle in.
As the sun lowers and the sand cools, enjoy swimming and snorkeling.
Photograph the volcanoes and sandbar in the low afternoon light.
Return to the terminal with time to spare before the last boat.
Have dinner while watching the sunset from a beachside restaurant or your lodging's terrace.
The afternoon course works best when the sea is calm, as in
March–June
. During the northeast monsoon from
November to February
, the waves sometimes build as the afternoon goes on, so choose the morning course.
The fastest route is a Cebgo direct flight from Cebu to Camiguin Airport (CGM), with a flight time of about
50 minutes
. From Manila, connect via Cebu, or take a direct flight from Manila to Laguindingan Airport (CGY) in Cagayan de Oro (about
1 hour 30 minutes
) and continue by bus and ferry. The Camiguin route has few seats and frequent schedule changes, so check the airline's latest timetable.
Camiguin Airport lies west of Mambajao town, about
6 km
by road from the boat terminal. A tricycle or multicab gets you there in about
15 minutes
From Laguindingan Airport, go to the Agora bus terminal in Cagayan de Oro city and take a bus to Balingoan. It takes about
2 hours
and costs about
The ferry from Balingoan port to Benoni port on Camiguin takes about
1 hour
and costs about
one way. Boats generally run from around
to around
, so it is safest to reach Balingoan by
at the latest.
From Benoni port to Yumbing, where the boat terminal is, is about
24 km
along the island's north coast road. Either take a jeepney to Mambajao (about
30 minutes
, about
) and switch to a tricycle, or hire a tricycle or multicab at the port and go straight there in
40–50 minutes
. A RoRo ferry also runs about once a day between Jagna on Bohol and Balbagon on Camiguin, taking about
4 to 4.5 hours
; check the operator's latest notices.

items.title: From Mambajao to the boat terminal

children.text: The terminal is about
8 km

by road west of Mambajao town, right next to Paras Beach Resort in Barangay Yumbing. It is easy to find by entering the resort's name or "White Island Ferry Terminal" in a map app, and a tricycle takes
15–20 minutes
. Agree on the hire fee, including the return trip and waiting time, before you set off.
To explore the island freely, you can rent a motorbike for about
a day (fuel extra). Park it near the terminal and board the boat, and always wear a helmet.

items.title: Crossing to the sandbar by bangka

children.text: At the terminal ticket office, pay the entrance fee of about
per person plus the boat fare. A bangka costs about
round trip for up to six people, so if you are traveling alone, sharing a boat with other travelers cuts the cost. The crossing takes about
10 minutes
Boats generally run from
to

, and the boat that took you over comes back to pick you up. Agree on a return time with the boatman before you get off. Fares and hours can change, so check the price list posted at the ticket office first.
White Island can be visited year-round, but
March–June

, with little rain and a calm sea, is best. Clear skies show the volcanoes' outlines sharply, and boats are rarely canceled. At midday in this season, however, the sand gets too hot to walk on barefoot, so go in the morning or late afternoon.
July–October
brings rain spread evenly through the months. Mornings often clear after a passing shower, so it helps to keep a spare day in your plans. Around the third week of
October
, the Lanzones Festival is held in Mambajao and accommodation across the island fills up fast.
From
November to February
, the northeast monsoon brings frequent rain, and on some days bangkas cannot sail to the sandbar off the north coast because of the waves. Late typhoons sometimes cross northern Mindanao around
December
, so check the forecast. In this season the sun rises around
and sets around

The size of the sandbar depends more on the tide than on the season. At high tide the edges go under and it narrows considerably; at low tide the sand is widely exposed and sometimes seems to connect to the small sandbar opposite. Check the low-tide time in a tide app the day before your visit.

items.label: Meals
items.note: Per meal at a beachside restaurant

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.

Accommodation is concentrated in Yumbing, where the boat terminal is, and neighboring Agoho beach. Staying at a beachfront place facing the sandbar lets you walk to the terminal for the first boat, which makes a sunrise visit much easier. Simple guesthouses are said to cost about
per room per night and beach resorts with pools about

; prices rise and rooms fill quickly during the Lanzones Festival and Holy Week. Paras Beach Resort, right next to the terminal, is a long-established beach resort that also serves as a landmark for finding the terminal.

There is no guarantee that anything is sold on the sandbar, so bring water and light snacks, and carry all your trash back. For meals, use the beachside restaurants in Yumbing and Agoho or eat in Mambajao town. Grilled fish, kinilaw (raw fish dressed in vinegar) and squid dishes are common, at about
a meal. Camiguin pastel — soft buns filled with custard or ube cream — is worth buying in town to take on the morning boat, and around
October
, when the Lanzones Festival is held, lanzones are easy to buy at roadside stalls and markets.
If possible, take the first boat around
. With fewer people and lighter wind, it is good for both photos and swimming.
Bangkas are priced per boat. If you are alone or a pair, ask other travelers at the ticket office whether they want to share a boat.
Check the low-tide time in a tide app before going, and you will see the sandbar at its widest.
There is no shade, so bring a hat, sunglasses and a long-sleeved rash guard, and use reef-safe sunscreen to protect the coral.
Bring plenty of bottled water. There is no drinking water and no toilet on the sandbar, so take care of things before you set off.
The sand gets hot at midday, and the shallow bottom is mixed with coral fragments. Wear aqua shoes or thick-soled sandals.
Put your phone and camera in a waterproof pouch or dry bag. Spray flies when the bangka crosses the waves.
The entrance fee, boat, umbrella and gear rentals are all paid in cash. Bring plenty of ₱50 and ₱100 notes.
Take a photo of your boat's name or number so you can find it easily among the many boats on the way back.

The sandbar has no trees, no shade, no drinking water and no toilets. At midday the sun reflected off the sand and water is extremely strong and heatstroke comes easily, so keep your stay short and drink water often.
There are spots with fast currents on the outer side of the sandbar and along the edges where it gets deeper. Do not swim far out alone, and wear a life jacket when snorkeling.
Hibok-Hibok is an active volcano that is still monitored. As of the check on
November 13, 2026
, Hibok-Hibok was not listed in the alert status of the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS), but the situation can change, so check the latest notices.
During the northeast monsoon from
November to February
, or when a typhoon is forecast, boat service can stop suddenly. Do not schedule the sandbar for the morning of the day you leave Camiguin.
At high tide the edges of the sandbar go under quickly. Leave bags and shoes in the middle, away from the waterline.
Do not touch or take coral, shells or marine life. Please also refrain from taking sand.
Official fee notices are hard to confirm, so prices on site may differ from this guide. Check the fares posted at the ticket office, whether they are per person or per boat, and keep your receipt.

Yumbing, where the terminal is, sits on the island's ring road, so it is easy to continue anywhere from here. For a guide to the whole island, including hot springs, waterfalls and Mantigue Island, see this entry.
About
7 km
from the terminal along the west coast road,
15–20 minutes
by motorbike. With its white cross at sea and the Guiob Church ruins, it suits an afternoon plan or sunset viewing.
About
6 km
by road from the terminal,
15–20 minutes
away. A warm spring rising at the foot of Hibok-Hibok, it is a good place to relax after a morning on the sandbar.
About
11 km
from the terminal,
25–30 minutes
away. A waterfall dropping straight down the hills south of Mambajao, with a cold pool to cool off in.
The gateway to Camiguin. It takes about
2 hours
by bus to Balingoan and then about
1 hour
by ferry, so staying a night there before or after your trip makes things easier.
